inline.s: Liu Kuan of the Han dynasty was exceedingly forgiving toward those beneath him. Even in haste, he never used harsh words or wore a wrathful look. His wife wished to test him and make him angry, so she waited for the hour of the court assembly when he had finished dressing in full ceremonial garb, and sent a maid to carry him soup, who deliberately spilled it and soiled his court robe. Liu Kuan said slowly: Did the soup scald your hand? His expression did not change.

A man named Hu Tai had a mother of a most cruel nature. Whenever she beat her bondmaids, the pain and torment were beyond words. Ten years after her death, the father had married again. One day, when Hu Tai was out, the household wanted to slaughter a chicken. The chicken suddenly spoke in human language, saying: Do not cook me; wait until the boy Tai comes home. Presently Tai returned, and the chicken circled his seat, murmuring to itself. Because of her cruelty to a bondmaid, she had been reborn as a chicken, and it told the family affairs in great detail. Tai wept and told his father, and they kept the bird for a long time, until it flew up and pecked the second wife. When Tai went out, the second wife struck it dead. Alas! Today there are a great many chickens and dogs. Who knows whose wives they once were? Pitiful and terrifying.

Wang Jianyi, marshal of Hongzhou, suffered from an illness in which adverse qi attacked the heart. He died and then revived, and told his wife: I once had a young bondservant who, because I restrained him too harshly, came to his death. Just now I arrived at the underworld, and the young bondservant lodged a complaint against me. It could not be settled. My present illness is precisely his mischief. His wife said: How would a young bondservant dare to do such a thing? He answered: In the yang world there are noble and base, but in the courts of the dead all are one. Soon afterward he died.

There are two kinds of intimidation. One is to meet a person in urgency or danger, to give him no comfort, but to make a show of force and stir up his terror. The other is to seek profit or work off a grudge by putting on a false display of power, making him fear me, in hopes of getting what I want. I have heard that Bodhisattva Avalokitesvara, amid terror and urgent distress, can bestow fearlessness upon living beings and thereby attained perfect penetration; this is foremost. Therefore the beings of Jambudvipa all call him the Giver of Fearlessness. If that is so, how should one behave in intimidating others? Thus the noble man, whenever he meets someone in a place of terror, never fails to strive to comfort him. It is a pity the world does not know this, and takes pleasure in frightening people. After one death, such a one is born as a river deer. Now the river deer is a creature that by day shuns and fears the beasts, starting up in flight at the least thing; by night it hangs its horns on a branch and sleeps curled like a bow, and wakes to find its four feet scrambling in fright — frightened again, sleeping again, sleeping again, frightened again, from dusk to dawn without one moment of peace. Such is its recompense.

A small merchant of Huzhou was selling ginger at Yongjia. A rich man named Wang, quarreling over the price, struck him angrily on the back and he fell to the ground dead. He was hastily revived by first aid, and Wang apologized and gave him a bolt of silk. The merchant returned as far as the river mouth, where the boatman asked where he had gotten the silk. He told him everything. The boatman then bought the silk and the ginger basket from the merchant. After the merchant left, the boatman dragged in an unclaimed corpse, brought it to his own house, and went to knock at Wang's door, asking: This afternoon a merchant of Huzhou crossed the river and said that you had beaten him and he was near death, and he begged me to call his parents, wife, and children and report it to the officials, leaving the silk and basket as evidence. Before I could turn on my heel he breathed his last. I dared not fail to inform you. Wang's whole household wept in terror and bribed him with two hundred thousand cash. The boatman made a show of reluctantly agreeing to their request, and together they buried the corpse deep in the woods. Wang had a servant who laid a complaint at the county office. Wang died in prison. The next year the ginger merchant came again and sought out his house. The son took him for a ghost, but the merchant said he had not died, and had now come with a small gift to thank him. The son then kept the guest, seized the servant, and accused him before the magistrate. The boatman was arrested. Both died in prison.

The world of Jambudvipa has always been called defective. How can a man have everything to his liking? When things do not go as he wishes, it must be because his accumulated merit is thin and therefore his enjoyments are thin as well. He should only keep to his lot, reflect on his faults, and cultivate the heavenly nobility. This is the excellent way of the ages for dwelling in poverty, and the excellent method for seeking good fortune and avoiding calamity. Complain against Heaven and Heaven grows angrier; blame others and others grow more resentful. Not only is it of no benefit; it does harm besides.

Jiao Junming passed the examinations in his early years, but for a long time was not promoted. Again and again he complained against Heaven for his rough road, and he submitted a memorial with prayers. That night a strip of plain writing fell before his stove. Looking closely, he saw it was a heavenly seal-script of sixteen characters. Junming had heard that Lady He, the immortal, possessed the Way, and went to ask her. She would not speak. Junming pleaded bitterly, and at last she said: You received five ounces of gold, and ten years were deducted. You put a man to death unjustly, and after death you will be dealt with. Have you done these things? Jiao was speechless and could not answer.

When Zhang Dun of the Song was chief minister, he banished the chief councillors of the Yuanyou era to Lingnan. Fan Chunren was among them. Chunren was then already seventy, yet on hearing the order he cheerfully set out on the road, and he constantly warned his sons that they must not harbor the least resentment. Whenever he heard that any of his sons resented Zhang Dun, he would angrily stop them. Once, on the road, their boat capsized in the river and Chunren's clothes were soaked through. He turned and said to his sons: Was this Zhang Dun's doing too? This case of Lord Fan is wholly the learning of rejoicing in Heaven and knowing destiny. If a man can comprehend this principle and accept it calmly and rest in it, there will naturally be no complaining against Heaven or blaming of others.

Wind and rain are the work of creation, and each has a spirit in charge of it. Confucius would change countenance at a sudden thunderclap or fierce wind. The Book of Rites says: If there be a violent wind, a sudden thunderclap, or a heavy rain, one must change countenance; even at night one must rise, dress, and sit upright. Master Cheng would rise whenever wind and rain came, out of reverence for Heaven. Ignorant people, when rain is plentiful, complain of flooding; when it is clear too long, they complain of drought; when the wind is fierce, they complain of violence — never reflecting that yin and yang each have their fixed measure, and that sometimes officials are harsh and cruel, sometimes the people create karma, and either can bring untimely weather. How dare they curse and revile it? They only add to the sin of defying Heaven.

At the prefectural school of Xianning county in Zhending, the steward Yang Kuan was serving wine at a public banquet when he saw two whirlwinds in the corner of the wall. He poured a libation of wine to them. On another day, when he went with a group to burn incense at Mount Tai, he met two soldiers who invited him to drink; they parted without asking names. The next day, climbing the mountain, he came to a shrine and saw two soldiers whose appearance was exactly like those who had invited him to drink. He was greatly afraid. At the inn he again saw the two soldiers, who said to him: Have no doubt, sir. We two are attendants of the Emperor of the Mountain. One day we were sent on an errand past your honorable district, and were favored with your gift of two ladles of wine. Yesterday we therefore repaid you with a cup of wine. Having spoken, they vanished.

In Ezhou of the Song, a woman was washing a clay basin by the river when a sudden downpour soaked the road. She let out foul words cursing Heaven. At once a strange wind seized the woman and swept her into the river. Her husband urgently rescued her, but the clay basin had split in the middle and was stuck on her head like a cangue; to remove it brought pain to the marrow of her bones. Onlookers filled the doorway. After several days she could not bear the agony and died.

When people have a dispute or lawsuit, one should earnestly counsel and reconcile them, so that great matters are made small and small matters are made nothing; then both families receive the blessing. But to stir them up and set them fighting, or secretly to incite them, or to step forward as a witness, or to draft petitions and accusations for them, or to take the whole affair into one's own hands at the yamen so as to fish for profit in the midst of it — this calls down the wrath of the spirits and the resentment of men, and is the very depth of doing evil and wronging one's conscience. When the retribution arrives, there are those who cannot bear its bitterness and repent too late.

Liu Yuanzhi developed a carbuncle on his back, and neither medicine nor arts availed. The physician said: Human efforts are exhausted; I fear there is a heavenly calamity. Yuanzhi had a Daoist priest petition the Dipper. That night he dreamed a spirit said to him: You have violated the laws of Heaven; petitioning the Dipper cannot avert it. Yuanzhi answered that he was innocent of any crime. The spirit said: You lodged in a certain family and stirred up a lawsuit, so that two families were ruined. Yuanzhi said: It was my younger brother Yuanli who did it, not I. The king ordered an official to review it, and it was indeed so; he was therefore spared. The next year Yuanli died. The retribution for instigating lawsuits has in every case been cruel; seen with the eyes and heard with the ears, it is unmistakable. I earnestly counsel the people of the world: every trade can make a living — why must you take up the pen of the pettifogger? Recently I saw the Record of the Dark Court of Loudong, which tells of a litigation-master who came to the underworld. The king of the dead said: Though your karma was evil, yet when you wrote your plaints you always urged people to settle their quarrels and never to accuse falsely, and in your documents you often secretly lightened the charge. Because of these good thoughts, you are for the present pardoned and sentenced to life. Let those who have already taken up this trade and cannot change be warned by this; perhaps they may be somewhat healed.

A certain village schoolmaster of Xiuning was poor but diligent in study, and fond of reading the law codes. A rich man in the village died, and his two sons fought over the estate. The elder wished to sue the younger, and brought a generous gift to ask him to draft the plaint. The master said: I study the law in order to judge cases in years to come. How could I stir up a lawsuit for an elder brother? He spoke fully of the deepest affection of brothers and of how contention brings ruin to both, to warn him. The elder was moved to awakening. When the younger brother came, he too admonished him, and the younger yielded. So they became as fond of each other as before and prospered together. One day, while trading in sandalwood planks, they suddenly saw the master's name carved on a plank. The brothers awakened and said: We owe it to his counsel that our quarrel was settled and we were fortunate enough to establish our household. So great a kindness has never been repaid; therefore Heaven wrote his name there to show it to us two. They agreed to go home and sell that plank, giving all the price to the master. Reaching home, they sold it for three hundred ounces of silver. At that time the master was old and had no school, and father and son were eating wheat porridge together, when the two men came in with the silver and bowed, telling him the whole matter. The master at first declined, but the two said: It is a gift from Heaven. In the end they gave it to him.

Yu Tieqiao said: If one holds office, one should severely punish and prohibit those who instigate and delight in lawsuits. If one lives in the countryside, one should with pains counsel and stop those who have sued and those who have not yet sued. This is the foremost task for nourishing the vital spirit. Such a one is a great minister of the state and a great minister of Heaven and Earth.

Xie Qiu loved to do good deeds. By nature he did not contend, and he hated litigation. When a neighbor encroached on his land, someone urged him to go to the officials. Qiu explained it himself, saying: He may seize the land, but he cannot seize Heaven. In all things he was gentle and generous, and mostly of this kind. He lived to seventy-five; his sons and grandsons flourished, and some became eminent.
The Song to Quell Litigation says:
Never start a lawsuit; your household will decay.
Though you win ten thousand troops, you lose three thousand horse yourself.
The pettifogger shakes a soft stake; the witness demands a heavy fee.
Where is the honest clerk? And where the scribe who works for nothing?
The judge's ruling is unknown; you stand in dread as on the brink.
And if your foot should slip, the shame cannot be hidden.
I often hear of men who ruined their estate, and most did so fighting over land.
I have seen men sue over family property and only ruin their brothers.
In anger you frame the plaint; once sued, you suffer more anger still.
Greedy for gain you go to law, and lose both principal and profit.
A marriage turns to enmity, and kin are cast aside for nothing.
Robbed and then dragged before officials, you pay out double again.
Out of righteous zeal you contend for others, and in the end you lose all righteousness.
For a relative you thrust your head out, and from then on friendship is severed.
The scholar misreads his books; the craftsman forgets his trade.
The farmer lets his fields go wild; the merchant throws away his business.
The rich man is made poor by litigation; the poor man is made dead by it.
Small matters you do not settle; great matters you flee and hide from.
The false at last comes true; what ends hard began easy.
Wearied strength and toiling mind — what delight, what savor is there?
For a while your spirits are high; who will bear the bitterness afterward?
I counsel the people of the world: never make a lawsuit your plaything.
Unless the enmity is irreconcilable, never entangle yourself in one.
These homely words are detailed and sure; hold them firmly in mind, I beg you.

Reckless means giving no thought to whether a thing is right or wrong. Following means trailing after others. In great matters, when ministers of state form factions and cliques, grasping at court power, openly censuring and secretly undermining one another; and in small matters, when ordinary people join societies and swear brotherhood, becoming one another's wings, drawing in their kind and calling to their friends — these are all reckless following and partisanship. There must be great sin and deep calamity in it. Ministers and commoners alike should firmly guard against it.

Liu Zongyuan and Liu Yuxi of the Tang were men of towering talent and unmatched learning, their names foremost in their age. It happened that Emperor Shunzong fell ill and could not speak, and the petty man Wang Shuwen suddenly grasped the great affairs of state. The two men threw themselves in and attached to him, lightly following and drawing one another on, believing that a Yi Yin or a Duke of Zhou had come forth again, so urgent and eager that they seemed mad. They were vaulted up to the post of attendant censor, and the whole court eyed them askance. Before long Shunzong passed the throne to the crown prince, Wang Shuwen's affair came to ruin, and the remonstrating officials attacked them in memorial after memorial. Both were banished as marshals of outlying prefectures and died in misery on the distant frontier. Alas! Had Liu and Liu not fallen into Wang Shuwen's party, their writings and their talents and character would still have made them famous ministers of a generation. One moment's slip of the foot, and a whole life could not rise again. How could one fail to be careful? Yet this is the lesser harm. The disorders of the Tang, Song, and Ming dynasties in three ages all began with this. Therefore the planting of parties by ministers is a crime of the greatest weight.

A son of an old family, poor and of no good conduct, often kept company with an actor. The actor repeatedly gave him clothes, and so they became the warmest of friends. Warm friendship made him learn that the actor was a thief. Later he wore the clothes he had gotten and went to market, where the owner seized him and brought him before the officials. The actor had already fled far away, and in the end he could not clear himself. He died in prison. Again, the son of a wealthy man loved boxing and staves, and swore brotherhood with ten men. His father, knowing of it, said they might bring the village to order, and did not forbid it. Later one of them turned thief, and when the affair was exposed, the confession implicated the rich man's son. Because the family was wealthy, the officials actually convicted him as a receiver of stolen goods, and the household was ruined. Alas! Let those who follow parties and make companions take warning from this.

Yu Que, Duke Zhongxuan of the Yuan, said: If a man draws near the worthy and good, it is like a sheet of paper; wrap orchid and musk in the paper, and it gains fragrance from the fragrance. If a man draws near wicked friends, it is like a willow branch; string fish and turtles on the willow, and it gains stench from the stench. In establishing ourselves and living in the world, we ought to repeat these words three times.

The words of wives and concubines are sweet and easily enter the heart; the instructions of parents are upright and hard to follow. There are none of the words of wives and concubines that do not run counter to the instructions of parents. This is why filial piety decays in the world because of wives and children. Now parents have seen and lived through much, so their view of affairs is sure to be right; and their love for their children is deep, so their plans are sure to be thorough. How could a young woman's view ever surpass that of a man ripened by long experience? This holds for the principles of things as well; it is not only said to urge filial piety.

Zhang Gongchen said: Even if a man followed his parents' instructions ten thousand parts, in the end he still would not have followed them. And of the words of wives and concubines, men say they do not listen in the least, yet in the end they use them all. Reason cannot overcome desire, and what is near at hand blinds a man so that he cannot see it. Let the self-willed fellows who think well of themselves not take this passage lightly. Without fine and close attention in the heart, a man can neither practice it nor even understand it.

Wives and concubines are a man's helpmeet within the home. If they have good words, there is no reason one may not follow them. But women who are worthy and clear-sighted are few, while the dull and benighted are many; and their nature is often narrow and willful, impatient of affairs, and they are clever at glossing over strengths and weaknesses, their words striking exactly the mark. A husband is most easily bewitched by them, and once bewitched by a woman's words, he is sure to turn against his parents. Therefore the Most High strictly warns against it. As for estranging flesh and blood, driving away relatives, cheating and bullying one's neighbors, showing partiality to one's own children, and oppressing servants and bondmaids — the source of these is mostly the wife. One should examine each matter as it arises and lead her on with the Way. And when a husband uses a concubine's words to abuse or cast off his wife, this above all is what human feeling is most prone to be partial in and most easily bewitched by; one cannot but be careful. That the Most High speaks of wives and goes on to concubines has good reason indeed.

A son toward his parents should exhaust his heart and strength, and east, west, south, or north, follow only their command. How can he answer them with drift and hesitation, consenting outwardly while refusing inwardly, and turning his back on their instructions? This is a root offense and an unpardonable evil. And when a man turns against his parents because he dotes on wife and concubines, the world is by no means lacking in such people; their crime is one degree greater. May everyone read this volume thoroughly, repent of former faults, and early plan to repay them: establishing himself and conducting himself, wholly reverent and wholly providing, to repay the agony of their toil by one part in ten thousand — then perhaps he will not fall within reach of the thunderbolt of Heaven, the slaughter of ghosts, or unforeseen calamity.

Cheng Yanzun served his mother with the utmost filial piety. His mother's nature was exceedingly stern, and she hated Yanzun's wife and drove her out. Yanzun was then in the prime of manhood, but he complied with his mother's will and never married again his whole life. His wife, though worthy and driven out, never uttered a word of complaint, and at the seasons sent greetings to her mother-in-law, living alone and keeping her chastity unchanged. The scholars and gentlemen thought her worthy and wrote a Record of Filial Fidelity. Alas! This may be called a filial son and a virtuous wife, with nothing to add. Could those rebellious sons and shrewish daughters-in-law fail to die of shame?

In Wen'an county a certain resident took a wife who was beautiful but fierce in her treatment of her mother-in-law. When the husband came home, she would always complain that the mother-in-law abused her, and the husband always kept silent. One evening he brought out a sharp knife and showed it to his wife. She asked what it was for. He said: You complain that my mother abuses you. Shall we take this and go together? She said: That is what I wish. The husband said: You had better serve her well for a month, so that all the neighbors know how diligent you are and how cruel she is. Then we will do it secretly. The wife did as he said, with cheerful face and gentle words, serving her morning and evening. Nearly a month passed. He took up the knife again and toyed with it under the lamp, and asked his wife: How does my mother treat you now? She said: Not as before. Another month passed, and again he tapped the knife and asked. The wife said joyfully: My mother is now very fond of me. What we spoke of before, do not do it. The husband slowly gripped the knife and glared at her, saying: Have you seen a husband kill his wife in this world? She said: Yes. He said: Have you seen a son kill his mother? She said: I have never heard of it. The husband said: In human life, supporting one's parents with filial piety is the greatest thing. The grace of parents cannot be repaid even by death. And when a man grows up and takes a wife, it is precisely in order to serve his parents-in-law and continue the family line. I have watched you again and again: you cannot comply with my mother, and instead you would make me a great rebel. This knife was truly meant to cut off your head to gladden my mother's heart. I have spared you for two months, to let you mend your ways and show a pleasant face, fulfilling the way of a wife, and to make plain my mother's heart toward you, so that you may know the fault is not hers, and then shut your eyes and receive the blade. The wife trembled, wept, and bowed, saying: Spare me from death, I beg you. I will comply with my mother-in-law all my life and never dare slacken. After a long while he consented. Thereafter wife and mother-in-law were harmonious, and the story spread through the village. This man of Wen'an was nothing but an ordinary fellow, yet he was skilled at turning and transforming, changing evil into good, which even scholars and gentlemen are sometimes unable to do. The saying goes: In the world there are no parents who are in the wrong. And it also says: In the world there are no parents who cannot be transformed. How true, how excellent!

Shen Zezhi at twenty-five gave up study to seek profit. His wife, of the Shi family, was worthy, and earnestly remonstrated with him, but he would not listen. So she spoke bitterly to her parents-in-law, saying: The new brides and sisters-in-law here were all married to scholars. Now my husband will not read, and if I return to visit my family I am ashamed to face my relatives. I wish to provide the tuition myself. I beg you to choose a teacher for him and press him to study. I do not dare hope for eminence, only that he become a good licentiate, not shaming the family, and that will be a worthy husband. Her parents-in-law agreed. Five years later Zezhi indeed passed the examinations and rose to the office of senior secretary. Those today who drag their husbands down into evil — why do they not take the worthy wife of the Shi family as their model?

Liu Jiande's wife was fierce and wicked, and Liu could not control her; he mostly obeyed her. It happened that his mother fell ill, and the wife had her sent to a nunnery. The mother did not wish to go, but Liu listened only to his wife and merely sent a bondmaid to attend her broth and medicine. As the mother lay dying she cursed loudly: I will surely complain in the courts of the dead. Within a few days the wife went mad and cried out: I did wrong to drive my mother-in-law to the nunnery. The dark court is drawing out my guts and flaying my skin. Her whole body turned black and purple, and she died. Two days later Liu also went mad and cried: I am Liu Jiande. Ruled by my wife, I defied my own mother. My wife has already had her guts drawn out and her skin flayed by the dark court and suffers in the uninterrupted hell. Now they are pursuing me urgently. Let the people of the world take warning from me: do not be bewitched by wives and concubines and defy your parents. He died suddenly. After the coffins had lain several days, a peal of thunder suddenly split both coffins open, and the stench carried for miles. Now the five punishments comprise three thousand articles, and no crime is greater than unfilial conduct; this is the king's law, and everyone knows it. But as for the thunderbolt of Heaven that strikes down, it is always rebellious sons and rebellious daughters-in-law, and of these people may sometimes be unaware. I write this to proclaim it to all under Heaven.

In small things, clothes and utensils; in great things, the bonds of friendship and kinship; within, wives and concubines; below, young servants and bondmaids — all have the new and the old. To gain the new and forget the old is the extreme of shallowness and want of kindness. A former worthy said: Rather than form a new friendship, it is better to deepen an old one. How excellent are these words! Long ago the king of Chu issued an order seeking a lost shoe, saying: I grieve for the one that went out with me and did not come back in with me. From that time no man of Chu dared cast off the old. Truly he was a man of feeling for all ages and a man who knew the Way for all ages.

The elder sister of Emperor Guangwu of the Han, Princess Huyang, was newly widowed and wished to marry Song Hong. The emperor said to him: The rich make new friends, the noble make new wives — is this not human nature? He answered: The friends of poverty and low estate must not be forgotten; the wife of the chaff and husks must not be put from the hall. The emperor turned to the princess and said: The matter will not come off. Reading this, I sigh and say: To pity the new and cast off the old is the way of all the world, and between wives and concubines a man is most easily moved. Often resentment grows on the pillow and disaster is bred in the women's quarters, with harms that cannot be spoken. How can a man fail to be careful?

A wealthy man had no son. He had already adopted his brother's son and raised him for ten years, when suddenly a concubine bore him a son, and the old man cast off his brother's son, and the whole estate went to the concubine's son. Later the brother's son established a household by diligence and thrift, and was filial, fraternal, respectful, and kind, so that the whole clan praised him. But the concubine's son, when grown, was dissolute, visited prostitutes, and gambled away everything they had. The old man died vexed and regretful.

Jing Yang of Yizheng, in poverty, was on friendly terms with Shi Cheng of Yangzhou. When Yang died, his orphaned children declined, and the relatives and old friends of former days would have nothing to do with them. Cheng alone did not forget, and constantly sent greetings and gifts, more than in former days. Yang had left several tens of scrolls of writings, and Cheng donated a thousand pieces of gold to print them, saying: I cannot bear that the finest essence of an old friend should perish in the ground. Later Cheng rose in office to high rank.

Fan Wenzheng of the Song, while prefect and vice director of the Ministry of Personnel, had three bondmaids attending him. Until he had served in two administrations and finally died — ten years in all — he never added one, nor ever lightly exchanged them.

When heart and mouth are both upright, one is a man of pure goodness. Even when heart and mouth are both crooked, men may still guard against him. But one who speaks of Yao and Shun while his heart is that of Jie and Zhou, who swears by mountains and seas while harboring pitfalls in his breast — such a one is hardest to fathom. In serving his lord he is sure to be disloyal; in serving his parents he is sure to be unfilial; in making friends he is sure to be faithless; in dealing with subordinates he is sure to be unrighteous. Such people are the worst of petty men. If they make others wrongly believe their words and fall into their snares, their crime is several times that of open evil. The Buddhist scriptures say: One who speaks falsely and reviles with his mouth, when he dies, falls into the hells of the pulled-out tongue, of molten copper, and of the plow of fire. When immeasurable kalpas of suffering are finished, he is born among the animals, forever eating thorns and brambles; and if he becomes a man again, his tongue is defective, his breath always foul, and though he speak good words, no one believes him. The karma of the mouth being one thing and the heart another gains such retribution. How can one fail to guard against it?

Xue Wenqing of the Ming said: The Book of Changes says, Sincerity in ordinary speech. Ordinary speech men take to be of no importance, and so they let it out carelessly and without caution. They do not know that one false word is a failure of speech. Therefore ordinary words must be sincere; this is the fullness of virtue.

Sima Wengong of the Song, showing Liu Qizhi the essentials of wholeheartedness in conduct, said: It is only sincerity. And its practice begins with not speaking falsely. Master Sima also once said that Qizhi's whole life was simply the one word sincerity, which no beating can break. At that time the townspeople and old farmers said that if one passed through Nanjing and did not see Attendant Liu, it was like passing through Sizhou and not seeing the Great Sage. Why did he move people so? It was also said: It was only sincerity. From this we see that the word sincerity never misled anyone. Why will men not strive at it?

Ren Guozuo had long been ill and held a Daoist offering to pray for aid. In a dream Ren heard a spirit say: Ren Guozuo, all your life you have been one thing in heart and another in speech. From youth to manhood you have not one good deed. Your sins are already fixed; you will die within the day. And indeed he died. Now earth has no fixed position, yet the five elements take it as their master, the four seasons rely on it to proceed, and the ten thousand things depend on it to be born. Among the five constants, it is sincerity. If the four beginnings lacked sincerity, they would not make up benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom. Therefore it is said: Sincerity is the beginning and end of things; without sincerity there is nothing. People today, in the words they utter, speak to no one with a true heart — how can they ever complete themselves as human beings? If from this moment they awaken and change, making word and deed one and inside and outside answer to each other, then they will face affairs calmly and always have room to spare, with no shame before Heaven above nor shame before men below. Is this not joy? Yet this is what we are most prone to offend in, and where guarding against it is hardest. By no means relax the least bit, and cut yourself off from the land of light and uprightness to enter a realm of darkness and thorns.

To take without satiety is called greed. To be muddled and shameless is called presumption. To be loyal in serving those above and honest in holding oneself is the great principle of a minister. Now men deceive those above out of greed and presumption: where then is the principle of a minister? Even if for a time they gain wealth and honor, in most cases ruin follows on their heels and their sons and grandsons come to grief. How much better to be loyal and honest and keep oneself, seeking to preserve both person and name! As for yamen clerks who embezzle money and grain, estate stewards who conceal taxes and rents, and all such abuses — they are too many to enumerate. All amount to those below taking the wealth of those above, by scheming to conceal and cleverly deceiving. Yet the wealth so taken was in origin destined to be theirs; only because the road by which it came was crooked, both person and wealth are lost. How much better to be scrupulous in the least particular, so that the wealth that was theirs will come by some other and upright share, and they may take and hold it just the same. But the distance between safety and danger is far indeed. This is a truth of the highest order, and men should not be blind to it.

Wang, grand censor of Guizhou in the Ming, was governor-general of the two Guang provinces. In auditing the treasury he found a surplus of three hundred and forty thousand taels of silver, already written off by the Board of Revenue, with military pay fully disbursed, and no owner to whom it could be returned. It was because the long peace had lasted so long that soldiers were few and pay plentiful, and by daily and monthly accumulation this had come about; no one could trace from where it had come, nor did the court know of it. The duke found it and wished at once to memorialize and report it. None of his household dared speak. An old friend who had studied with him calmly asked: Not a speck of dust stains you, my lord; court and countryside alike know it. But this silver was neither taken from the people's fat below nor stolen from the state's revenue above. You have four worthy sons; might you make a little provision for them? Report three hundred thousand in gold and keep forty thousand to divide among the four young gentlemen; it would do no harm to your integrity. The duke laughed and said: Your words are reasonable too. But for a widow of thirty years to change her chastity in her white-haired age, once she begins to plan for her sons and grandsons — would that not be a turn to the left? In the end he reported the whole sum and kept not a farthing. Afterward the duke served successively as prefect, and his grandsons took the highest places in the examinations one after another, holding pure and important offices in unbroken succession — they were the brothers of the grand historian Xueyuan. Alas! Duke Wang may be called a man of difficulty, and a true noble man of the world.

In the Chenghua era of the Ming, Qin Hong was grand coordinator of Shaanxi. The guards and officers of the Qin princely house ran wild, and the people suffered under them. Hong seized and punished them all without the least leniency. The prince of Qin memorialized that Hong had insulted and destroyed a princely house of the imperial clan. The emperor was angry and had him arrested and thrown into the imperial prison, ordering the eunuch Shang Heng to confiscate his property. Only one bolt of yellow silk and a few old garments were found. Heng reported to the throne the state of Hong's poverty, and the emperor himself examined his possessions and sighed in admiration for a long while. He ordered Hong released from confinement and bestowed ten thousand strings of cash to commend his honesty, and transferred him to be grand coordinator of Henan. When he arrived at his post, the eunuch Wang Zhi also came on business. At that time Wang Zhi's power and prestige shook all around, and the other grand coordinators all bent propriety to see him. Hong alone paid his respects uprightly. Wang Zhi knew of his loyalty and honesty, and treated him with added respect. Hong secretly memorialized that Wang Zhi had brought many guards and officers and disturbed the local districts. Later, when Wang Zhi returned to the capital, the emperor asked him whether the provincial governors were worthy or not. Wang Zhi singled out Hong as honest and capable. The emperor showed him Hong's memorial, and Wang Zhi knocked his head on the ground and confessed his guilt, praising Hong's worth without end. The emperor let it pass. Hong afterward rose to be minister.

Yan Maoyou of the Ming said: In conduct and integrity reaching this point, a man is like the bright moon or blazing flame, like fine gold or beautiful jade. Is this not excellent? Had Duke Qin accumulated a little wealth and goods, then once thrown into the imperial prison, could he have been so free and easy? His honesty and authority once awe-inspiring, the eunuchs were shorn of color. Those before whom the Earl of Weining and Minister Yin knocked their heads and begged for pity — and Duke Qin, a distant official, blunted their edge. Alas! Noble or base, it lies wholly in how a man places himself.

Du Yan of the Song was a man of Shanyin. When he ate at home, he had only one dish. Someone said he was too frugal. The duke said: Yan was originally a poor scholar. Rank, position, fortune, and emolument, cap and sash, dress and use — all belong to the state. Once they leave my person, I am a poor scholar again; how should I provide for myself? Now frugality is the method of honesty. When things press upon a man and circumstance constrains him, he gradually loses his freedom; extravagance and waste and reckless luxury all come from this. Even if he wished to be honest, could he? Therefore for honesty nothing is better than frugality. When governing the people, be as when at home; use the state's wealth no differently from your own. Then it will do.

A certain provincial administrator of Shaoxing prefecture was clever at greed and gluttony, and accumulated wealth to several hundred thousand. When he lost office and went home, he bought a hundred thousand mu of fine fields, the richest in the whole commandery. His grandfather and father appeared to him repeatedly in dreams, saying that the punishment of the dark court was about to fall, but he did not believe it. He had only one son and one grandson, and they indeed gambled and whored without repentance, and both died young. The administrator himself soon contracted paralysis, and his son's wife and grandson's wife gained a measure of ill repute; those who coveted his wealth flocked to them like ducks. The administrator lived to see it, and by the time he was near death the household was already emptied. As he was dying he opened his eyes wide and cried: My office rose to provincial administrator, which is not small; my fields reached a hundred thousand mu, which is not few. What I set up with my own hands, I have finished with my own hands. I do not understand it. Having spoken, he died. Alas! This is only the flower retribution; the fruit retribution lies in hell, and who knows what that is like. Excellent were the words of Yang Boqi: Though I have no rich estate to leave my sons and grandsons, so that later ages call them the descendants of a clean official, is what I leave them not great indeed?

Even when a man has faults, one should bend to shield him. But when a man is plainly innocent of any wrong, and someone fabricates rumors and invents evil deeds to slander him, the poison of it is worse than axes and wolves. For the man had no crime, yet one man blows the reed-pipe and a crowd of petty men bay like dogs, and the hearers are bewildered and cannot tell true from false, so that worthy and villain are confounded and dismissal and promotion are turned upside down. This is what the noble man condemns utterly. The Buddha said: The karma of evil speech, when one dies, falls into the hells of sword and spear and of the pulled-out tongue; and while alive one suffers in full the retribution of being butchered and of bodily mutilation.

An old poem says: Never listen to slander; to listen is to knot up calamity. Let a lord listen and his minister is put to death; let a father listen and his son is cut off. Let husband and wife listen and they part; let brothers listen and they separate. Let friends listen and they grow distant; let flesh and blood listen and the bond is severed. A stalwart frame of seven feet — do not listen to a three-inch tongue. On the tongue there is a dragon spring sword that kills without blood. Such is the harm of slander and calumny. Those who hear words — how can they fail to be careful?

Zheng Xuan said: Vulgar speech is close to the marketplace; mincing speech is close to the harlot; jesting speech is close to the player. If a noble man touches even lightly on these, he not only loses dignity but also breaks his blessing. How much more so with evil words?

Chen Liangmo of the Ming said: I once went as a subordinate official to Gong'an county. There was an instructor named Bai who went to the capital for the metropolitan examination. His wife loved goodness, and once, in the instructor's name, submitted a memorial and gave a Daoist nun one ounce of silver and ten feet of silk gauze for an embroidered banner. It happened that the wife of a colleague came to visit, and seeing it cried out in alarm: A scholar-official trafficking with a Daoist nun is no small matter. Bai's wife then believed that her husband's office was ruined from then on, and brooded over it. When the instructor returned having failed the examination, he took this silk gauze to cut a garment, and it too was snipped. His wife grew more uneasy and hanged herself. I heard of it at the time and asked the county magistrate, who told me the whole story, and I could not but pity Bai and grieve for his wife. Later the grand coordinator Lin Ershan, in a council to list the worthy and unworthy, said to me: Instructor Bai debauched the wife of a school clerk, and when his own wife spoke of it, he forced her to hang herself. His crime admits no pardon. I then told him what I had heard. As the duke pondered, I said: I do not know from whom the earlier report came. If it was indeed a noble man, perhaps it may be believed; if not such a man, I beg you to inquire further. The duke suddenly struck the table and said: That is it, that is it. He at once seized his brush and struck it out. Later Bai was promoted to assistant instructor in the Imperial College, and I was transferred to the Fujian judicial commission. I met Duke Ershan at Pu, and he pointed to a neighbor's house and said to me: This man of the Wu family was formerly assistant instructor at Gong'an; he is the one who slandered Instructor Bai. His heart and methods were never good, and so I awoke at once because of your words. He was later promoted to instructor at Pingxiang and was slandered by a colleague in the same way, dismissed, and on his way home crossing Lake Poyang his boat capsized and he barely escaped with his life. Now he is utterly desolate. The saying goes: Those who love to talk of the women's quarters and of the various shortcomings of others will surely rouse the anger of ghosts and spirits; if not a strange calamity, then a strange poverty. How much more so with Instructor Wu, who slandered and stained an innocent man! His retribution must be more than this. Yet the method of hearing words lies only in examining the man who brings them — is this not clear indeed?

In establishing himself and conducting himself, a noble man should act according to what lies within himself, and must make himself upright and without crookedness; this is uprightness. But if a man cannot be upright himself, and merely takes slandering others as uprightness, then his conscience is already lost — how can that be called uprightness? Moreover, an upright man's heart must be loyal and generous: he speaks when he ought to speak, so that others may know to mend. The point is that sincerity is abundant while words are few — this is what is called uprightness. Those who slander others stain their names and give vent to their own anger, and then call themselves straight-spoken. Is this not pitiable and hateful? Laozi said: Cleverness and deep insight that draw near to death belong to those who love to mock and criticize others. Cheng Yichuan said: Toward others, a noble man should seek the faultless within what is faulty, and should not seek faults within what is faultless; but toward himself he should reverse this. Alas! The people of the world commit endless karma of the mouth; therefore the Most High warns against it again and again.

Wang Wei, vice minister of the Ming, had been promoted through the recommendation of Yu Qian, the junior guardian. He waited for a fault or error of Lord Yu's and secretly memorialized to slander him, in order to buy a name for uprightness. At that time Emperor Jing trusted Yu Qian wholly and singled him out, and summoned him in and gave him Wang Wei's memorial. The duke knocked his head on the ground and confessed his crime. The emperor said: I know you myself; bear no grudge. When he came out, Wang Wei met him below the hall and asked what the imperial decree concerned. The duke would not speak. When he pressed again, the duke laughed and said: If I have done wrong, you should tell me to my face; I might not refuse to follow. How could you bear to go this far? Then he brought out the memorial and showed it to him. Wang Wei was terrified and ashamed, squirming with nowhere to put himself, and the duke laughed and comforted him.

Yang Tieya of the Yuan was held in the highest esteem throughout the land. At Linjiang there was a shrine to the Lady Wang, who had kept her chastity, and Yang inscribed a poem there: The armored horses plod on a hundred li; the blood-written letters were finished in the green maples after nightfall. It should only be that the peach-blossom waters of Liu and Ruan are not like the clear Han waters of Baling. Later Yang had no son. He dreamed of a woman who said: The poem you wrote on the Lady Wang, though it cannot harm the lady's name, yet your heart was cutting and unkind, and Heaven has cut off your descendants. Yang repented and wrote another poem: Heaven grows old with the earth; your handmaid follows the soldiers. Heaven and earth are heartless, but your handmaid has feeling. Biting open my finger, the blood reddens the rosy peaks; the moss traces turn to the green of the snow river. I would die amid the sound of the Xiang zither; I will not live to the beat of the barbarian reed. In the third month the cuckoo cries until its blood is spent; in the autumn wind there are no tears to write the mourning inscription. Again he dreamed of the woman, who said: Since you have repented, you shall have a son. And indeed a son was born. From this Master Tieya advanced in cultivation and attained the fruit of immortality.

Clear-sighted and upright is what is called a spirit, and a noble man should revere and fear it. Yet there are petty men without any sense of awe who claim to be upright and without crookedness and think they can bend ghosts and spirits to their will, not knowing that the subtle workings of their hearts have long since been seen through by the ghosts and spirits; they only bring guilt upon themselves.

Cui Hao of the Later Wei served Emperor Taizu of Wei and was favored with extraordinary honor, rising to the office of minister of education. Because in compiling the history he exposed and published the state's evils, he was condemned to death. Earlier Cui Hao had reviled and destroyed the Buddhadharma. His wife, of the Guo family, reverently loved the inner scriptures, and Cui Hao in anger took them all and burned them, throwing the ashes into the privy. When Cui Hao was imprisoned, he was put in a cage, and soldiers were set to urinate upon him. Since ancient times no chief minister who was slain and disgraced had ever suffered as Cui Hao did.

A cake-shop keeper of Zhenjiang surnamed Yu had a young son who died of smallpox. Yu actually wrote a petition to accuse the smallpox god before the City God's court. His wife snatched it from him and burned it at the stove. That night he dreamed that ghost officers seized him and dragged him off. The City God said: Your household's stove god has reported you. You have a petition accusing the smallpox god — what crime should that deserve? Yu said: The smallpox god demanded offerings and, when he did not get them, brought my son to death. In a moment the smallpox god arrived and said: That child's life was due to end — what has it to do with me? The City God judged: For the present, in consideration of the ignorance of a common man, send him to Magistrate Yang for twenty strokes of the rod and a month's illness. At that time Yang Shuting was magistrate of Dantu. The next day Yu was hanging up the door-latch at his gate when he damaged the official umbrella, and received twenty strokes of the rod. He lay ill in bed for a month and then recovered. Now the spirits and the king's law go together as complements, and so those who offend the spirits often find themselves offending the king's law as well.

Shi Que of Wei in the Zhou dynasty said: The lord righteous and the minister dutiful, the father kind and the son filial, the elder brother loving and the younger respectful — these are the six accordances. The base encroaching on the noble, the young insulting the elder, the distant estranging the near, the new estranging the old, the small adding to itself against the great, and license destroying righteousness — these are the six reversals. To cast off accordance and follow reversal is to hasten calamity. The Book of Documents says: Those who comply with virtue meet good fortune; those who follow reversal meet misfortune. It also says: Those who accord with Heaven flourish; those who defy Heaven perish. According with it, one is loyal and filial, a sage and a worthy; defying it, one is mad and violent, a rebel and a bandit. The raising of the thought lies in a single instant, and fortune and calamity are divided as widely as sky and earth. How can one fail to be careful?

Zhao Fengzi of Wen'an county in Bazhou was a man of courage and strength. Together with Liu Liu and Liu Qi he divided the roads as a bandit, plundering Henan and entering Biyang, where he dug up all the tombs of the ancestors of Jiao Fang, saying: Let me put this villain to death with my own hands and so thank the world. Afterward he was defeated by the government troops and turned to raid Lu'an, and the government troops again pursued and attacked him. Fengzi seized a monk's ordination certificate, shaved his head, and pretended to be a monk, but was captured by his subordinate general Zhao Cheng and cut to pieces. Liu Liu and Liu Qi reached Mount Wolf at Tongzhou when a sudden hurricane arose, and the bandits were all annihilated. Now there are two kinds of reversal. One is that of ministers and sons who turn against lord and father. The other is that of robbers and bandits who disturb and harm the villages. The defiance of ministers and sons — disloyalty and unfilial conduct — has been set out above with its law and its warnings in full; therefore here we speak only of the lawless bandit, wishing men to keep to their lot and follow reason, and so preserve their bodies and lives.

To turn one's back on kin and incline to strangers is not confined to one kind. For example, to deceive and turn one's back on one's parents and secretly entrust oneself to a wife's family; to treat one's parents' kin with cool indifference while being generous to a wife's party; to haggle over every farthing with brothers while being openhanded with friends and outsiders; to ignore the poverty of one's own clan while falsely claiming kinship with another line — all cases of making light of what should be held dear and holding dear what should be made light of are of this kind. Confucius said: He who does not love his kin but loves others is called one who defies virtue. He who does not revere his kin but reveres others is called one who defies propriety. Now to turn one's back on kin and incline to strangers comes either from settling old scores and grudges out of selfishness, or from looking to who is in power and who is out of favor. The defiance of virtue and propriety is extreme. This is a root crime of weight, and the retribution must be severe.

Zhou Cong, having repeatedly failed the examinations, went to Qiao commandery and paid homage to the commandery clerk Zhou Ji as his father, daily taking his place among his sons and using that family's three generations of names in full. The next year he passed the examination by this means and did not return home. His own father reproved him with a poem, and Zhou Cong died of shame.

Bai Xi of the Ming had no son, and would not take his nephew as heir; instead he adopted the son of a butcher. Later Xi died. A traveler lodged in his house, and at night heard sounds of running about; he rose and looked through the crack of the door, and saw several men and women pacing back and forth and looking around, with the look of hunger on their faces. Then he saw one man with a butcher's knife thrust in his belt stagger in, and after a little while come out with a full belly. The men and women stamped their feet and said: We are suffering, we are finished, again we get nothing to eat. And they withdrew in anguish. When it was light he asked the servants, who said: Last night the head of the house sacrificed to the ancestors. Then he understood: the one holding the butcher's knife was the boy's birth father, and the men and women were the ancestors of the Bai family, and Xi and his wife. The man sighed and went out.

Heaven and earth are without partiality, and the spirits are upright. Accord brings good fortune, defiance brings misfortune, and the response is like an echo. Even with a careful and reverent heart a man still fears he may offend; how much less should he dare to invoke and call upon them to witness his own petty and sordid concerns? Is this not a defilement? Would Heaven and earth and the spirits ever help a man to do evil? He only hastens his own calamity.

In Zhang Zhong's family, perverse qi gathered in one household. Between father and son, brothers, mother-in-law and daughters-in-law, sisters-in-law, there were quarrels at every turn, and they would often call on Heaven and earth and invoke the spirits, wishing to clear themselves. When the day came to divide the household, the strife grew worse, and they set up rival offerings to the spirits and made curses against one another. From then on monstrous hauntings arose frequently and illnesses came again and again, and within a few years they had nearly all died out.

Master Lianchi of the Ming said: In the world's making of vows — as when praying for a son, for long life, for deliverance from danger, for fame and office, for wealth and emolument — one must never vow to slaughter animals and offer them as sacrifice. This is called an evil vow, having sin and no merit. Even when vowing robes, banners, the building of halls, or the setting up of offering vessels, one should only take it as adorning the teaching of the images, and as wishing all beings to gather their hearts in reverence and awe. One must not deliberately seek blessing. Now great compassion and equality is what is called Buddha, and uprightness without partiality is what is called spirit. If a man seeks blessing only out of selfish heart, would Heaven and earth and the ghosts and spirits ever send down auspiciousness in return for a bribe? Judged by principle, it lies only in each man doing his utmost in his own heart and broadly practicing all good: loyalty and filial piety, friendship and brotherly love, pitying the poor and cherishing the old, relieving disaster and succoring the suffering, abstaining from killing and setting creatures free — all manner of hidden virtue, all manner of skillful means, according to his lot and ability, done with all his strength. Where good deeds move them, blessings naturally descend. But if a man does no good and merely gives rise to prayers and longings, then it is a petty and sordid concern, and a defilement of the spirits. I proclaim it to all the world: believe these words firmly.

In the matter of giving, merit is established most swiftly. Yet one must love goodness without wearying, and only then is there progress. Even if one's means fall short, one should still keep this heart always; how much less may one lose the first thought for the sake of a moment's stinginess! To regret before giving means the gift is never made; to regret after giving means one gives no more. This robs benevolence and harms righteousness, and is the root of the sickness of the heart. Therefore the Most High does not record the good of such a man's giving, but picks out only the evil of his regret. For what the sage prizes most is nothing other than turning to good and mending faults, and what he hates most is nothing other than doing good without persisting to the end.

As for one who regrets after giving: trace it to the beginning, and in the end his joy in goodness was never true. It was no more than a passing excitement, a seeking of fame and blessing. The source was already wrong — how could he not regret? But one who gives with a true heart and sees self and other both as empty will never come to this. Therefore one who does good must be able to discern at the very sprouting of a single thought.

Fu Ya took joy in giving, and beggars filled his gate. He often said: The wealth of the world is not fixed. Today rich, tomorrow poor — it turns like a ring. If I go a single day without giving, my heart is not at ease. People of the time made a saying of it: Rather than grow rich as Quan, be poor as Fu Ya. Later he rose to be director of the secretariat, and his sons and grandsons grew richer still.

Liu Kuan loved to give to the poor and needy, laboring without weariness. Later he was enrolled by the Most High as a marquis and commander of the Hall of the Youthful Beginning, in charge of those who have just attained the Way.

Shi Bingzhi of Yongqing, digging earth to build a house, found several tens of thousands of taels of silver. He sighed and said: Wealth is man's life. Since Heaven has bestowed it, how can I enjoy it alone? Whatever could relieve the poor and those in urgent need, he did without fail. Later, in a year of famine, he brought out eighty thousand piculs of grain to relieve the starving people. Before long bandits swarmed like bees, and he again scattered his family wealth to protect the village. The authorities reported it to the throne, and he was granted office and a memorial arch. He lived to ninety-four, and his sons and grandsons flourished.

Zhang Xianke of Wujin was compassionate by nature and loved to give. He once gave away three thousand coffins, and afterward continued giving. He hired beggars to bury the corpses beside the roads, paying a fixed sum for each corpse, and the beggars rejoiced whenever they found a body left in the open, taking it for merchandise. From then on there were no unburied corpses in the district. He also boiled medicinal ointment to give to the sick, and in cold weather made porridge to feed the hungry, saying: If I bury the dead, how can I fail to keep the living alive? His two sons passed the examinations and received titles of honor. Now dearth and famine are calamities, and poverty and hardship are destiny. To relieve calamity is the heart of Heaven and earth; to create destiny is the learning of sages and worthies. These several men, by giving with a sincere heart, obtained blessing, long life, wealth and honor, and descendants; and they were reborn in good places. This is the principle of things.

Xi Baisan was originally a poor man. He once saw a Daoist priest begging at a shop, and the shop would not give. Baisan felt at his waist and had only one coin left, and he gave it. That night he dreamed that the Daoist removed his wen. When he woke, the wen on his jaw had indeed fallen off. The gift of a single coin actually freed him from the suffering of illness. From this we see that giving does not lie in the amount of one's strength but in the heart. The people of the world should each strive with a single heart, and urge others to do the same; even then they would think it too late — how much less may they regret!

Lending and borrowing serve to circulate what is had and what is lacking, and to relieve what is urgent. It is a fine thing. The one who receives the kindness is already greatly obliged; how then can one use force and refuse to repay, or use cunning to shift and evade? Do they not know that an unpaid debt from a former life must be repaid after death — lightly, by becoming the man's servant or bondmaid; gravely, by becoming his donkey, horse, ox, or dog in repayment? This too is to be feared.

Whenever one borrows another's things, one must take extra care of them. When borrowing from others, unless it cannot be avoided, one need not borrow at all. When the borrowing is done and the use finished, return it at once. In this way one is not only not resented by others, but also has no shame before himself. As for borrowing and lending money, one must above all repay others clearly. In this world there are many who borrow and do not repay, never reflecting that the wealth is not their own: even if they keep it, in the end it goes. And when the wealth is gone, only the debt remains. What good, what good is there in it? I beg you to think on this.

In the autumn of the wuwu year of the Kangxi era of the Qing, a resident of Yanjing named Zhang Yuan kept a donkey that could travel two hundred li a day. It loved to kick and bite people; only when Zhang and his two sons rode it would it be docile. No one else could ride it. It happened that a man named Yang tried borrowing it as an experiment, and it submitted quietly to the reins, so he rode it out. When he returned, Yang dreamed that a man in black told him: I am the Zhang family's donkey. In a former life I borrowed three hundred coins from you and did not repay them, and now I must make compensation. Yesterday you rode me two hundred and eighty li; I beg you to ride me twenty li more, and my account will be settled. Yang asked how much money he owed the Zhangs. The donkey frowned and said: Much, much, much — it cannot be told. Yang woke, and indeed borrowed the donkey again and rode out. When he had gone a little farther than before, it suddenly threw Yang to the ground; by the reckoning of the road it was exactly twenty li. Yang was all the more amazed, and prayed: I understand now. But I am still ten li from my lodging; if I do not ride you, how can I get back? When we return I will buy ten coins' worth of hay to feed you — how is that? The donkey stood and looked at him a long while, then again became docile and went on. Afterward Yang deliberately tried it again, and as soon as he came near the saddle the donkey kicked and bit and brayed long.

Zhu Zaian said: Among men there are those who are poor and in debt, and those who are rich and in debt. To be poor and in debt is a matter of insufficient strength. If one follows the Scripture of the Middle Admonition and diligently thinks of repaying, one will naturally be without fault. But as for having means and not repaying, either one is using borrowed authority and relying on power, or else one is blind to reason and has lost one's heart. Who knows that life after life, the repayment is only then finished?

A certain merchant Wu of Huizhou held to faith and righteousness. As he lay dying he showed his two sons, saying: All the silver I have exactly matches what I have borrowed. Repay every item to the full. Better to suffer hunger and cold than to be a man who betrays his heart. His sons obeyed their father's command in every particular, and lived in poverty and hardship. Then one day, in a dry well, they found two thousand taels of silver, stamped with a reign title of the Tang. They shut the doors and hid it closely, and no one knew of it. The next day a man from a neighboring county suddenly arrived, saying: Are you not the sons of Wu? They said: We are. He said: Great wealth has come to you. A few days ago, when I was ill, I went to the palace of Mount Tai, and saw at the treasury office a man delivering money who called himself the spirit of the well spring. The officer in charge said: This is silver from the Tang dynasty's inner treasury. The Most High, because Wu's dealings with wealth were clear and honest, and his sons have painfully kept their father's will, gives this sum to them, to enjoy great wealth in the world. I was astonished when I woke, and so I have come to pay you a visit. The brothers were amazed and told him the truth. Today the Wu family is exceedingly wealthy, and all are of his descendants.

The reason men do not keep to their proper lot is simply that they say scheming and seeking are profitable. But let them consider: in human life, wealth and honor, poverty and low estate, are fixed and unchangeable; noted in the dark and received in the light, all is former karma. How can one scheme and seek beyond one's lot? A deluded heart and greedy thoughts, hoping for a lucky chance, are not only useless but may even break one's blessing through delusion. Why not embody Mencius's words that one seeks it by a proper way and obtains it by destiny, and the sixth patriarch's that all fields of blessing are not apart from the square inch of the heart?

At the beginning of the Changqing era of the Tang, Pei Pu, magistrate of Xinping, died. His elder cousin Hua Yuan was then lodging in Longyou, and on the road he met a military officer with a great retinue of riders — it was Pu. Amazed and delighted, he said: Elder cousin, you have left the world — how is it that you hold a military post? Pu said: My office is that of the Abrading Envoy of West Sichuan, in charge of the increase and decrease of the world's wealth. In the world, every drink and every bite is foreordained — how much more so wealth! What is registered in the dark court has a fixed limit; beyond the limit, I abrade it away. Whether a man wastes it himself, or meets with disaster, or loses in trade, or has it scattered by illness, all comes under my abrading office. In the world, the farmer toils for grain, the merchant toils for wealth, the scholar toils for emolument, and each obtains only what belongs to his lot; he does not add to what is not in his lot, and if he is not diligent he even loses what is in his lot. That you have met me is also foreordained. You are due two catties of white silver; beyond this, whatever I gave you I would have to abrade again, and so I dare not give you much. Having spoken, he vanished.

Liu Hang was quite able in letters, and promised himself early success in the highest examinations. At that time the True Lord Yisheng descended and spoke at Mount Zhongnan, and Hang took the occasion to ask him. The True Lord said: Your writings are indeed superior, but your destiny is shallow. If you rest content, withdraw, and keep to your lot, you may preserve your remaining years; to seek beyond will surely shorten your life. Hang could not follow it, and in the end accomplished nothing and died. Now the matter of the examinations, which brings glory to ancestors and blessing to descendants, cannot be obtained by clever scheming; yet the diligent practice of hidden virtue can bring it about amid what is unseen and unheard — how could that be called seeking beyond one's lot? It is the same with wealth.

Zhang Yue returned to dwell in his old home and shut his gate, not going out. Beyond this, public and private affairs alike he took no part in, and he increasingly honored frugality and thrift as an example to his sons and grandsons. He once had a saying posted on a screen: When a guest comes, keep him for a meal, frugal and suited to the occasion; dishes are set out according to what there is, fruit according to the season. Even for new kin there is no lavish feast; even for a great guest no beast is slaughtered. This not only guards against extravagance and makes for endurance, but will also spare one trouble and bring peace to life. Zhang Gongchen said: To be content in poverty and keep to one's lot, and to live frugally, frees one from seeking help from others; to reduce affairs and clear the heart, and to seek surplus, only brings suffering on oneself. In human life, blessings to be enjoyed are arranged by Heaven; plenty or scarcity, adversity or success, are fixed from birth. Even what wit and scheming may obtain comes only when the time and fortune are due. See through this device, and one gains how much ease! Wait until you have enough — whose enough is enough? When you can rest, then rest.

To press with force means, wherever one's power reaches, to put forth authority and devise means with all one's intent, leaving no margin at all, never resting until the advantage is pressed to the uttermost. It is what is called hauling the sail full of wind and adding eight more oars.

Xi Xiandu of the Liu Song dynasty was an attendant cavalier of the outer bureau. Emperor Xiaowu once had him supervise labor, and he was cruel and without principle, always beating and flogging, allowing no rest in the heat and rain or the cold and snow. Men could not bear it, and some hanged themselves. Xiandu too was exposed and put to death.

The scholar Qian Hetan of Huating was building a mansion in his retirement, and the labor was so heavy and bitter that the villagers were afflicted by it. One workman could not bear the service, and the duke angrily reproved him. The workman said: In former days, when Lord Huang the judicial commissioner was building his mansion, I was pressed into service and fell ill. Now the Huang house is already fallen and its walls ruined, while my illness is still not recovered; therefore I cannot answer the summons. Hearing these words the duke was greatly awakened, and at once stopped the work. Now for one in high place to press the common people, or for the rich and honored to press the poor and lowly, is of course to offend against the Most High's warning. But even to press animals with human strength is also impermissible. As for the ox and donkey that plow, the horse and mule that carry — if they did not gain their bodies by former cultivation, then they are creatures that owe me a debt. One should love and pity them, and not use them to the exhaustion of their strength, saying: They are animals, a different kind, and so I may do as I please with them.

Crooked conditions meeting from without destroy virtue and lose the heart — the Most High has already handed down the warning above. But even in the proper relations of husband and wife, one must above all have restraint. If one says that what is proper is not licentiousness, how shall one escape the calamity of indulging desire and destroying the body? Now the vital essence of the human body is dispersed in the three burners and makes the hundred vessels flourish. Once the fire of desire is stirred, it gathers and flows, all issuing from the gate of life. If the weir is not held, the vast sea is drained dry. This is most to be feared. In any man, when the essence is full, spirit is born; when spirit and essence are full, wisdom and thought are born, and he is intelligent and strong and firm — what can he undertake that he will not accomplish? But if in youth he cuts and destroys it, his heroic spirit fades away, and the work of a lifetime is gone.

A man's lifelong illness often begins from the time of his new marriage. Young and ignorant, he often gives free rein to passion without measure, and many become consumptive and frail, some even dying young and leaving their wives to bitter widowhood. Think — a marriage bond of a hundred years, a lifelong union: why suffer it that within one month a root of calamity for a whole life be planted? When fathers and elder brothers meet with sons and younger brothers about to marry, they should earnestly use this as a warning.

The saying goes: When joy reaches its height, sorrow is born; to indulge desire is to breed calamity. It also says: Few desires will surely give many sons; greedy lust often leaves no heir. Confucius said: When the blood and qi are not yet settled, guard against lust. Old Peng said: The highest adepts sleep in separate beds, the middling in separate coverlets; to take a hundred pills of medicine is not so good as sleeping alone. The Buddha said: Woman's beauty is the root of all suffering, the root of obstruction, the root of killing, the root of sorrow. The Scripture of the Yellow Court says: Urgently guard the chamber of essence; do not let it leak at random. Close it and preserve it, and you may live long. Truly, where lust reaches, nature is destroyed and the body perishes; there are those who secretly suffer its harm without knowing it, and those who clearly know its harm yet pay no heed. This is why sages and worthies warn of it so earnestly and repeatedly. Ordinary men do not know, and act without restraint; the qi of lust and filth angers the ghosts and spirits, and all manner of misfortune comes from it. I earnestly pray that all may endure and forbear in good time, and so obtain the way of long endurance; otherwise they will die for it and none can save them.

Ren Huigong grew healthier and stronger in old age. Someone asked him the art of nourishing life. The duke said: It was simply that in reading the Anthology of Literature I had an awakening. When the mountain hides jade, the mountain glows; when the water holds a pearl, the river is lovely — that is it. Cheng Yichuan held it a deep shame to forget oneself in pursuit of desire, and at seventy his sinews and strength were undiminished from his prime. Li Jue lived to a hundred, with a complexion like an infant's. When people asked his art, he said: I cut off desire early. Liu Yuancheng at eighty was still strong, and said of himself that he had been sparing of desire for thirty years, and his blood and qi and thoughts were just as they had been then. The monk Zhou of Luling was over ninety and walked long roads as if flying, his beard and hair not white. He said there was no other art: only that in his prime he had restrained desire. Zhang Cui of Taicang was over ninety, with sharp ears and eyes, and could still paint. Asked about it, he said: All my life my heart of desire has been faint and my indulgence restrained. Now to be old and yet strong is the first joy of human life, and what brings it about is no more than restraining lust and sparing desire. How hard is it for men to take them as models? Pengzu said: Once in a month, twenty-four times in a year. This is the way of restraint and care. Sunü said: A man of sixty should close and not let flow. This is the way of holding fast in danger. In this way one does not abolish the human way, nor damage the primal yang. I hold that in the time of Pengzu and Sunü men's vital endowment was thicker, and so they spoke thus. But in today's climate the atmosphere is very thin — how can one hold to this as the norm? And one whose primal qi is weak — how can he fail to be doubly careful?

A certain man surnamed Xu of Quzhou in the Ming was handsome and had a name for talent. Within twenty days he passed the metropolitan examination and was chosen as judicial officer of Songjiang prefecture. His relatives and friends envied him. But he loved beauty and kept more than ten exceedingly delicate and lovely concubines, indulging desire without measure. Within a month of taking office he collapsed and died, and all his concubines played a different tune.

A scholar Yu of Yin was handsome in figure and fond of lust. One night he dreamed that the City God reproved him; reckoning the number of his acts of lust, he was given several tens of strokes. When he woke, both his thighs were black and purple, and then they ulcerated. After more than a year of illness he died. Of ten thousand evils, lust is foremost; of a hundred virtues, filial piety is foremost. This is handed down as an iron case in the courts of Yama, and so the hatred of the ghosts and spirits for lust and their love of filial piety are extreme. Though the net of the yang world may let one slip, the law of the dark court is not remiss. How can men offend against what they hate? Therefore since ancient times no one who wallowed in women's beauty ever failed to lose his body and destroy his household. And for one advanced in years it is especially unfitting to take a young concubine. For I can no longer manage her, and she must hate me deeply; when the grudges of resentment accumulate, virtue is damaged and blessing is spent. And a young woman's temper is hard to manage, with yet more beyond this. How can one fail to guard against it? Moreover, with the sun's shadow already on the mountain, morning and evening are hard to preserve — yet one hastens to have the ghost officers drag one away. What folly!
Appendix: Master Qin Zhuo'an's days of abstinence for cultivating the person and establishing destiny.

The first day of the first month is called the Heavenly La. The Five Emperors correct the spirit, qi, emolument, and destiny of living men. Those who offend by lust have their emolument cut and their years seized. On the third, all the spirits assemble in the capital, and it is also the descent of the Dipper; those who offend have their years seized. On the fifth, the Five Voids. On the sixth, the Six Losses. On the seventh, the Upper Assembly. On the ninth, the Heavenly Birthday. On the fourteenth, the Three Primes descend, and it is also the birthday of the Heavenly Official of the Upper Prime; those who offend have their years seized.
